header.tag_why: Daniel framed this as 'an engineering decision', the opening question was 'how fast can we build this', and the deal stopped being a bake-off when a Fetchwell engineer built a working sitter payment flow in our sandbox over a weekend.

evidence.excerpt: They were launching Canada, then the UK, and sitters have to get paid locally.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Two engineers more or less full-time just keeping sitter payments working.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: a roadmap item, faster pay for sitters, that had been pushed three quarters in a row.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: a haunted house.
evidence.label: quote

trigger.insight: Expansion was the occasion, but the pain was engineering capacity: two engineers tied up on upkeep and a sitter-pay feature that kept slipping. The problem was what payments cost the team, not what payments cost in fees or declines. No one turned those two engineers into a money figure, and the buyer never needed that to decide.
trigger.messaging: Open on getting engineers off payments maintenance and shipping faster sitter pay in new countries, not on M1's global-currency line.

evidence.excerpt: Daniel. He signed.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this is an engineering decision, finance will sign what I bring them.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: The CFO joined one call for ten minutes, asked one question
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: does this change when sitters get paid?
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: The VP of Engineering owned the decision and finance approved what he brought. The CFO's only question was about sitter payout timing, not cost or ROI. The transcript never says what answer the CFO got.
decider.messaging: For engineering-led marketplace buyers, aim the pitch at the engineering leader and have a one-line answer ready for finance on how payout timing to sellers changes.

evidence.excerpt: I've stopped learning their names.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I know because the questions changed.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Do we lose PayPal, do we lose Venmo, what happens to the saved cards.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I assume Braintree told them they'd lose things. I don't know that. That's me guessing.
evidence.label: opinion

competitor.insight: The rep infers the Braintree call itself from the change in questions; it was not confirmed, and what Braintree said is pure guesswork. What is solid is that the customer's frame moved from build speed to loss aversion: PayPal, Venmo and saved cards. Daniel's line about account-manager churn is a people-continuity complaint. Our M5 tiered-response-times message does not answer it.
competitor.messaging: Pre-empt the 'what do we lose' question with a clear statement on keeping PayPal, Venmo and saved cards, and pitch support as people who stay on the account rather than as response-time tiers.

evidence.excerpt: One of their engineers, on her own time, built a working sitter payment flow over a weekend and showed it at Monday standup.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: And the marketplace piece. Onboarding sitters, the identity checks, paying out in local currency.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence: the acceptance-rate slide.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: our average booking is 38 dollars, I'm not losing sleep over auth rates.
evidence.label: quote

message.insight: M2 landed because the customer's engineer used the product, not because of anything said in the pitch. M11 drew interest. M4 fell flat: at a 38-dollar booking, Daniel dismissed auth-rate uplift, and the rep delivered the whole slide anyway. Nothing in the pitch spoke to the CFO's payout-timing question or the slipped faster-pay roadmap item.
message.messaging: Drop the acceptance slide for low-ticket marketplaces and replace it with a hands-on sandbox invitation plus the seller onboarding and local payout story.

evidence.excerpt: The weekend prototype. Before that it was a bake-off.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: After that Daniel stopped saying 'if.'
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I didn't even know until Daniel told me.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Only that I barely sold this. Their engineer did.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The turning point happened entirely inside the customer, and the rep learned about it secondhand. It is unclear whether the prototype came before or after the 'what do we lose' shift, so we don't know if it answered the Braintree-era doubts or just outweighed them. We have no customer statement of why they picked us over Braintree, only the rep's read and Daniel's change in wording.
decided.messaging: Make 'build a working flow in our sandbox this week' an explicit step in engineering-led deals instead of leaving it to luck.

evidence.excerpt: Nothing, really. It was a clean one.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: I didn't have a crisp answer on Venmo in the room, and I still don't.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: who's done this at our size without losing cards?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: we'll find out.
evidence.label: quote

gaps.insight: The rep first called it a clean deal, then admitted to dancing around PayPal and Venmo, having no Venmo answer even now, and never delivering the saved-card reference Daniel asked for. Those gaps did not kill the deal, but they carried into kickoff as untested risk. The rep says the customer chose to accept the risk, but that is her own read, not something the customer said.
gaps.messaging: Build a one-page proof on keeping PayPal and Venmo and migrating saved cards, plus a named reference at a comparable size, before the next marketplace deal raises 'what do we lose'.

evidence.excerpt: Payments shouldn't be a team
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: We want to stop babysitting this.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: paid by Friday
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: And nobody says 'payouts.' They say 'sitter pay.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: The customer talks about the burden on the team (haunted house, babysitting, payments shouldn't be a team) and a promise to sitters (paid by Friday). We talk in category words they never use: marketplace, payouts, authorization rates. The rep herself said 'the marketplace piece', which is our vocabulary, not theirs.
language.messaging: Rewrite M11 and the developer pitch in buyer terms, for example getting your team out of payments and keeping your promise on when sellers get paid, instead of 'marketplace payouts'.

gaps.question: Why did Fetchwell choose us over Braintree, in their own words?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel in a win interview what tipped it, and whether the PayPal and Venmo concerns were settled or just accepted.

gaps.question: Who was the incumbent provider?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya, or check the CRM, which provider Fetchwell is leaving and whether Braintree was the incumbent or a new contender.

gaps.question: Did Fetchwell actually meet Braintree, and what did Braintree say?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Daniel directly whether they met Braintree mid-evaluation and what prompted the 'what do we lose' questions.

gaps.question: What is our answer on keeping Venmo?
gaps.follow_up: Ask product or solutions engineering for a definitive Venmo position before Fetchwell's implementation reaches it.

gaps.question: What could we not show them?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya to deliver the saved-card migration reference Daniel requested, and confirm with the implementation team that no cards were lost.

gaps.question: What answer did the CFO get on whether sitter pay timing changes?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Priya what we told the CFO and whether it supports the 'paid by Friday' promise in Canada and the UK.

close.rep_takeaway: This deal was won by a customer engineer in our sandbox, and the rep only found out afterwards. On engineering-led deals, invite engineers to build early and stay close enough to know when they do. Also, a deal that feels clean can still carry open promises: an unanswered Venmo question and an undelivered reference became implementation risk, so close every 'I'll get back to you' before signature.
